about: GO in nine tenses. Built by scripts/build_turns.py from data/<lang>.json turnGrid plus authored status/marker/alt.

past.simple.note: la before the verb is the whole past tense; the verb leit never changes. Negative: ngam shym la leit.

past.progressive.note: la (past) plus dang (in the middle of). In a story the la is often dropped once the past is set: nga dang leit haba ...

past.perfect.note: la plus lah (already, completed). Usually paired with shwa ba (before) to mark the earlier of two past events.

present.simple.note: Bare verb: habit, fact, and also the present moment when dang is not needed. man ka sngi (every day) makes the habit explicit.

present.progressive.note: dang means 'still, in the middle of'. It is the only progressive marker and is used far less than the English -ing form.

present.perfect.note: lah alone before a verb means 'already done'. Experience ('have you ever') uses la ju: phi la ju leit? Not yet: ngam pat leit.

future.simple.note: yn fuses with the pronoun: ngan, phin, un, kan, ngin, kin. sa adds 'later': ngan sa leit. Negative: ngan ym leit.

future.progressive.note: yn plus dang. Rare; Khasi normally just says ngan leit with a time word (lashai, mynstep).

future.perfect.note: yn plus lah. For 'finished by' add dep after the verb and haduh (by): ngan lah trei dep haduh janmiet.

past.simple.note: Spoken German uses the Perfekt (bin gegangen); ging is the written Präteritum.

past.progressive.note: No progressive form: Präteritum or Perfekt plus gerade, or a rephrase such as unterwegs sein.
past.progressive.source: ich ging gerade / ich war gerade unterwegs

past.perfect.note: Plusquamperfekt: war/hatte + Partizip II. Used with nachdem, bevor and als to order two past events.

present.simple.note: The only present tense; it also covers 'I am going' and, with a time word, the future.

present.progressive.note: No -ing form; gerade or jetzt marks right now. 'Ich bin am Gehen' is colloquial and regional.

present.perfect.note: The Perfekt is the everyday past, not an English present perfect. 'I have been here since May' is present: ich bin seit Mai hier.

future.simple.note: Present plus a time word is the default; werde gehen adds a promise, a prediction or formality.

future.progressive.note: Does not exist as a form; use the present or werden with gerade or dann.
future.progressive.source: ich gehe dann gerade / ich werde dann gerade gehen

future.perfect.note: Futur II exists but is rare in speech; usually the Perfekt plus bis dahin does the job.
future.perfect.source: ich werde gegangen sein / bis dahin bin ich gegangen

past.simple.note: Perfective participle agreeing with the subject. जाना is intransitive so no ने. Also covers English 'I have gone' in most contexts.

past.progressive.note: Stem + रहा + past of होना. Both रहा and था agree with the subject in gender and number.
past.progressive.source: मैं जा रहा था / रही थी

past.perfect.note: Simple past plus था. Also used for a remote or completed-before-another-event past, and often where English says 'I went' with a time long ago.

present.simple.note: Habitual: imperfective participle + हूँ. Means what you regularly do, never what you are doing now.

present.progressive.note: Stem + रहा/रही/रहे + हूँ. Also the normal way to say a near-future arrangement: कल जा रहा हूँ.
present.progressive.source: मैं जा रहा हूँ / रही हूँ

present.perfect.note: Simple past + हूँ. Sounds bookish for most verbs; in speech people say मैं गया (हुआ) हूँ for 'I've been (to)', or use जा चुका हूँ for 'have already gone'.

future.simple.note: Synthetic future: subjunctive जाऊँ + गा/गी/गे. Used for predictions and promises; for fixed plans use the progressive or जाना है.

future.progressive.note: Progressive + future of होना. Doubles as the presumptive 'I am probably going' (see D-MUST-BE).
future.progressive.source: मैं जा रहा हूँगा / रही हूँगी

future.perfect.note: Simple past + हूँगा. In real speech it usually means 'I must have gone / probably went' (past presumption); for 'will have finished by X' people say तब तक जा चुका हूँगा.

past.simple.note: Passé composé with être for aller; the participle agrees with the subject (allée for a woman). The passé simple (j'allai) is never spoken.

past.progressive.gloss: I was going / I used to go
past.progressive.note: Imparfait: background, habit, description. j'étais en train d'aller exists but is heavy; the imparfait alone usually does the job.

past.perfect.note: Plus-que-parfait: imparfait of être/avoir plus participle. Used exactly like English past perfect, and obligatory in the third conditional (si j'étais allé...).

present.simple.note: One form for habit and for right now. aller is irregular: vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont.

present.progressive.gloss: I am (in the middle of) going
present.progressive.note: No progressive tense. en train de is a substitute used only when you must stress 'right now, mid-action'; most of the time je vais is enough.

present.perfect.note: Same form as the past simple cell: the passé composé is both 'I went' and 'I have gone'. 'I have been going for' is present tense plus depuis (je vais ... depuis deux ans).

future.simple.gloss: I am going to go / I will go
future.simple.note: aller plus infinitive is the spoken default for anything planned or near; the futur simple (j'irai) is for predictions, promises and more distant plans, and is compulsory after quand referring to the future.

future.progressive.note: Does not exist as a tense. Use the futur simple with a time phrase (à cette heure-là, je serai sur la route) or en train de if the mid-action sense really matters.

future.perfect.note: Futur antérieur: futur simple of être/avoir plus participle. Used with d'ici (by), and also for likely explanations (il aura raté son train, he must have missed his train).

past.simple.note: Perfekt only: the dialect has no Präteritum, so 'ich ging' does not exist. sii/haa too: ich bin gsi, ich ha gha.

past.progressive.form: ich bin grad am Gaa gsi
past.progressive.gloss: I was (in the middle of) going
past.progressive.note: No imperfect. Background is 'am + infinitive' inside the Perfekt, or just the Perfekt plus 'grad' (just then).
past.progressive.source: ich bin grad am Gaa gsi

past.perfect.note: Doubled Perfekt (Perfekt II): participle plus gsi/gha. Speech mostly uses plain Perfekt with 'scho' or 'vorhär' instead.

present.simple.note: One form for habit and now. gaa is irregular: gang, gasch, gaat, gönd, gönd, gönd. Standard 'ich gehe'.

present.progressive.note: 'am + infinitive' is the only progressive and is far more common than in Standard German (ich bin am Ässe). Otherwise use the present.

present.perfect.note: Same form as the past simple cell: the Perfekt is both 'I went' and 'I have gone'. 'Have been going since' is present plus sit (ich gang sit zwei Jahr).

future.simple.gloss: I will go / I am going to go
future.simple.note: Present plus a time word is the normal future. 'wird + infinitive' is for guesses (er wird scho cho) and promises, and is rarer than in Standard German.

future.progressive.note: No such tense. Present 'am + infinitive' plus a time word (dänn, am Achti) does the job.

future.perfect.note: No future perfect. Perfekt plus 'dänn scho' (by then already), or 'bis dänn bin ich ggange'. 'ich wird ggange sii' sounds bookish.
